katas.question:
Write a program that accepts a sequence of lines as input and prints each line with all of its characters capitalised. Input ends at the first blank line.

```

W 200
```

For example, given the input:

```
W 200

```


katas.title: Percent-encode a string
katas.question:
URLs only allow letters, digits, and the characters `-` `_` `.` `~`; every other character must be percent-encoded: replaced by `%` followed by the character code in upper-case hexadecimal.

Define a function `percent_encode(text)` that returns `text` with every character outside the allowed set encoded. For example, `percent_encode("!*'();:@&=+$,/?%#[]")` returns `'%21%2A%27%28%29%3B%3A%40%26%3D%2B%24%2C%2F%3F%25%23%5B%5D'`, and `percent_encode("Send a message")` returns `'Send%20a%20message'`.
hints: Test each character with `c.isalnum()` or membership in the string `"-_.~"`, and format the code with `f"%{ord(c):X}"`.

katas.title: Unwrap a Google redirect URL
katas.question:
Links in Google search results are rewritten to route through `google.com` before the browser follows them. Each rewritten link carries the destination, percent-encoded, in the `url` query parameter, like this:

```
https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&rct=j&q=&esrc=s&source=web&cd=&cad=rja&uact=8&ved=2ahUKEwjAhNDPz7zqAhVt_XMBHepeBf8QFjAAegQIBRAB&url=https%3A%2F%2Fmoz.com%2Flearn%2Fseo%2Fredirection&usg=AOvVaw0OxLud1UuZx_hO1HV9QrJ2
```

Define a function `undirect(link)` that takes a rewritten link and returns the original destination: the value of the `url` parameter, with `%3A` restored to `:` and `%2F` restored to `/`.
hints: Split the query string on `&` and `=`, look for the pair whose name is `url`, and decode it with `str.replace()` twice — once for `%3A`, once for `%2F`.

katas.title: Look-and-say sequence
katas.question:
The look-and-say sequence starts from `1`. Each later term describes the previous term by reading off its runs of identical digits: a run of `M` consecutive copies of a digit `N` is written as the count followed by the digit, so `1211` — one 1, one 2, two 1s — reads as `111221`.

Write a program that prints the first 8 terms of the look-and-say sequence, one per line:

```
1
11
21
1211
111221
312211
13112221
1113213211
```
hints: Keep the current term in a string, and repeat 8 times: print the term, then build the next term from it.
Walk the term with an index `i`: while the character after `term[i]` matches it, extend the run and count it; when the run ends, append `f"{count}{term[i]}"` to the next term and move past the run.

katas.title: Count each word in a text file
katas.question:
The text file `prose.txt` is supplied with this kata and listed in its Files tab. It contains the passage:

```
The quick brown fox jumps
over the lazy dog.
The dog barks; the fox runs away.

"Where did the fox go?" asked the dog.
Nobody knew, so the dog slept.
```

Write a program that reads `prose.txt` and counts how many times each word appears in the passage. Capitalisation is ignored, and a word is a run of letters: whitespace and punctuation both separate words, so `barks;` and `"Where` count as the words `barks` and `where`.

The program should print one `word,count` pair per line in first-appearance order:

```
the,7
quick,1
brown,1
fox,3
jumps,1
over,1
lazy,1
dog,4
barks,1
runs,1
away,1
where,1
did,1
go,1
asked,1
nobody,1
knew,1
so,1
slept,1
```
hints: Read the whole passage into a string with `f.read()` inside a `with open("prose.txt") as f:` block, then loop over its characters with `for c in text:`.
Build each word in a string `word`: when `c.isalpha()`, add `c.lower()` to it. Any other character means the word has just ended.

When a word ends, count it with `counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1` and reset `word` to an empty string. The last word is still in `word` when the loop finishes, so count it once more afterwards.

files.prose.txt:
The quick brown fox jumps
over the lazy dog.
The dog barks; the fox runs away.

"Where did the fox go?" asked the dog.
Nobody knew, so the dog slept.

tests.stdout:

quick,1
brown,1
fox,3
jumps,1

lazy,1
dog,4
barks,1
runs,1
away,1

katas.title: Parse a quoted CSV file without the csv module
katas.question:
A CSV file stores one row of values per line, separated by commas. A value that contains commas is enclosed in double quotes, and a double quote inside a quoted value is written twice: `"Austen, Jane"` holds the value `Austen, Jane`, and `"The ""Outsiders"""` holds the value `The "Outsiders"`. Double quotes appear only in these two roles.

The text file `books.csv` is supplied with this kata and listed in its Files tab. It contains:

```
"Emma","Austen, Jane"
"The ""Outsiders""","Hinton, S. E."
Animal Farm,"Orwell, George"
"Dune","Herbert, Frank"
```

Without using the `csv` module, define a function `parse_row(line)` that takes one line of the file and returns the list of values on that line. Use it in a program that prints each line of `books.csv` as a list. A quoted value never contains a line break.

The program should print:

```
['Emma', 'Austen, Jane']
['The "Outsiders"', 'Hinton, S. E.']
['Animal Farm', 'Orwell, George']
['Dune', 'Herbert, Frank']
```
hints: Walk the line one character at a time with an index in a `while i < len(line):` loop. Keep the value being built in a string, and a flag `in_quotes` that is `True` while you are inside a quoted value.
Outside quotes, a comma ends the current value — add it to the list and start a new one — and a double quote starts a quoted value. Inside quotes, every character belongs to the current value.

Inside quotes, a double quote followed by another double quote is an escaped quote: add one double quote to the value and skip both. Any other double quote ends the quoted value. Add the final value after the loop, and remove the newline from each line with `str.strip()` before parsing.

files.books.csv:
"Emma","Austen, Jane"
"The ""Outsiders""","Hinton, S. E."
Animal Farm,"Orwell, George"
"Dune","Herbert, Frank"

tests.stdout:
['Emma', 'Austen, Jane']
['The "Outsiders"', 'Hinton, S. E.']
['Animal Farm', 'Orwell, George']
['Dune', 'Herbert, Frank']

Define a class named `Person` with a class attribute `name` set to `"Person"` and an instance attribute `name` set through the constructor.

Create one instance whose name is `"Jeffrey"`, passed through the constructor, and a second instance whose name is set to `"Nico"` after construction. For each instance, print a line of the form:

```
Person name is Jeffrey
```

so the first line shows the class attribute and the second shows the instance attribute.
hints:
Set an instance attribute inside the `__init__()` method.
An attribute can be passed to the constructor or assigned later.

tests.stdout:
Person name is Jeffrey
Person name is Nico

katas.title: Caesar cipher class
katas.question:
A Caesar cipher replaces each letter with the letter a fixed number of positions down the alphabet, wrapping around: with a shift of 5, `'a'` becomes `'f'` and `'y'` becomes `'d'`. Punctuation and spaces are left unchanged.

Define a class `CaesarCipher` instantiated with an integer shift. It should implement two methods: `encode(text)`, which returns the text with each letter shifted, and `decode(text)`, which restores it.

For example, `CaesarCipher(7)` encodes `'If he had anything confidential to say, he wrote it in cipher, that is, by so changing the order of the letters of the alphabet, that not a word could be made out.'` as `'Pm ol ohk hufaopun jvumpkluaphs av zhf, ol dyval pa pu jpwoly, aoha pz, if zv johunpun aol vykly vm aol slaalyz vm aol hswohila, aoha uva h dvyk jvbsk il thkl vba.'`
hints:
Shift letters with `chr((ord(c) - base + shift) % 26 + base)`, where `base` is `ord('a')` or `ord('A')`.
Decoding is encoding with the opposite shift.

tests.stdout:
Pm ol ohk hufaopun jvumpkluaphs av zhf, ol dyval pa pu jpwoly, aoha pz, if zv johunpun aol vykly vm aol slaalyz vm aol hswohila, aoha uva h dvyk jvbsk il thkl vba.
If he had anything confidential to say, he wrote it in cipher, that is, by so changing the order of the letters of the alphabet, that not a word could be made out.

katas.title: Evaluate Q = √(2CD/H)
katas.question:
Write a program that calculates and prints values according to the formula:

`Q = square root of [(2 * C * D) / H]`

where `C = 50` and `H = 30` are fixed, and the values of `D` are supplied to the program as a comma-separated sequence. Round each result to the nearest integer and print the results as a comma-separated sequence.

For example, given the input:

```
100,150,180
```

the program should print:

```
18,22,24
```
hints:
If a result is a decimal, round it to the nearest whole number — for example, `26.0` should be printed as `26`.
Assume the input is supplied through the console.

katas.title: Robot's distance from the origin
katas.question:
A robot moves in a plane, starting from the origin `(0, 0)`. It can move UP, DOWN, LEFT or RIGHT by a given number of steps, and its movements are recorded in a trace like this:

```
UP 5
DOWN 3
LEFT 3
RIGHT 2
```

The number after each direction is the number of steps. Write a program that computes the distance between the robot's final position and the origin after a sequence of movements. If the distance is not a whole number, print the nearest integer. Input ends at the first blank line.

For example, given the input:

```
UP 5
DOWN 3
LEFT 3
RIGHT 2
```

the program should print:

```
2
```
hints: Assume the input is supplied through the console.

katas.title: HTTP date string
katas.question: When a browser and server communicate over HTTP, the protocol fixes a format for dates: `Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT`. Define a function `http_date(moment)` that takes a `datetime` object representing a GMT time and returns it in this format.
hints:
Build a fixed datetime with `datetime(1994, 11, 6, 8, 49, 37)`.
Format codes: `%a` weekday abbreviation, `%d` day, `%b` month abbreviation, `%Y` year, and `%H` `%M` `%S` for hour, minute, second.
